⁉️ Charles Schwab has expanded its cryptocurrency trading service to include Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink, allowing eligible US retail investors to buy and sell five digital assets directly through Schwab Crypto. The additions give customers access to more cryptocurrencies through the same platforms they use to manage stocks and other traditional investments, without having to open an account with a separate cryptocurrency exchange.

☄️ Joe Vietri, head of digital assets at Charles Schwab, said the company was responding to customers who wanted more flexibility in managing their cryptocurrency investments. At the time, cryptonews reported that the brokerage was preparing to expand its digital asset offering beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum, with the new tokens expected to become available in the following months. 

💭 The company had already begun offering direct cryptocurrency trading to selected retail customers in May 2026, before making Schwab Crypto available to all eligible retail clients in October. With the latest rollout, customers can trade SOL/USD, AVAX/USD and LINK/USD pairs through their Schwab Crypto accounts. Schwab said its selection of cryptocurrencies is based on customer demand and its preference for established digital assets. The company intends to introduce more tokens and other digital asset products over time, although it has not identified the next cryptocurrencies it plans to support.

➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

SoftBank is probably best known for its stories involving WeWork and some of the world's biggest companies. And it looks like the holding company has now reached a point where AI is no longer just a story about rising asset valuations, but a story about real debt.

The company has made a massive bet on AI. It has invested or committed to invest around $65 billion in OpenAI alone, while OpenAI and Arm now account for roughly three-quarters of the value of its key assets.

The problem is that a significant portion of this bet is being financed with debt. In September, SoftBank issued $11.1 billion in bonds, the largest high-yield corporate bond offering in history. Some of those bonds carried yields of nearly 10% annually.

And the market is already getting nervous. SoftBank shares have lost nearly half their value since the beginning of September, while the cost of insuring against a potential debt default has reached its highest level in four years.

The really uncomfortable part begins if AI asset valuations continue to fall. That would mean collateral loses value, borrowing becomes more expensive, and the company may have to sell assets to reduce its debt. And SoftBank owns a significant stake in Arm, is one of OpenAI's largest investors, and is financing massive AI infrastructure projects.

That's why SoftBank's problems could quickly stop being the problems of just one company. 
The pressure could spread to Arm, private AI company valuations, data centers, and eventually the entire tech market.

On Tuesday, November 10, SoftBank will release its latest quarterly earnings report. The main things to watch are its debt, cash position, and how the company plans to keep financing its AI bet.

Because if the next major AI crisis starts not with a stock market sell-off, but with debt problems at the biggest borrowers, SoftBank is one of the first places to look for signs of trouble.
